Duration: one and a half hours. Answer ALL the 50 questions in this examination. All questions carry equal marks. Calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is appropriate, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square bracket for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer, you will score a zero for that question). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. questions.enonce_markdown: The integrating factor of the differential equation $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{y}{2x}=\dfrac{e^{x}}{\sqrt{x}}$, $x\neq 0$, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ the integrating factor is $e^{\int P\,dx}$. Here $P(x)=\dfrac{1}{2x}$, so

$$\int P\,dx=\tfrac12\ln|x|\quad\Rightarrow\quad e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{\frac12\ln|x|}=|x|^{\frac12}.$$

For $x>0$ this is $x^{1/2}$. Option A is not of this form, and option B would be the integrating factor of $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+\dfrac{2y}{x}=\cdots$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{1}{e^{2i\theta}}\equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown:
By Euler's formula $e^{i\phi}=\cos\phi+i\sin\phi$, hence with $\phi=-2\theta$

$$\frac{1}{e^{2i\theta}}=e^{-2i\theta}=\cos(-2\theta)+i\sin(-2\theta)=\cos2\theta-i\sin2\theta.$$

The factor $e^{-2}$ in options A and D is a trap: the $2$ belongs to the argument $2\theta$, not to the modulus, which is $1$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The expression $\dfrac{x^{2}}{(x^{2}+2)^{2}}$ in partial fractions, where $P,Q,R,S$ are real constants, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The denominator is the square of the irreducible quadratic $x^{2}+2$. For each power of an irreducible quadratic factor the numerator is a linear polynomial, so the form is

$$\frac{x^{2}}{(x^{2}+2)^{2}}=\frac{Px+Q}{x^{2}+2}+\frac{Rx+S}{(x^{2}+2)^{2}}.$$

(Indeed $\dfrac{x^2}{(x^2+2)^2}=\dfrac{1}{x^2+2}-\dfrac{2}{(x^2+2)^2}$, so $P=R=0$, $Q=1$, $S=-2$.) Options A and D use constant numerators, which is too restrictive for a general form, and option C has a quadratic numerator, which is not allowed because its degree must be less than that of the factor. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The series $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty} r^{-\frac{k}{2}}$ is divergent for
questions.corrige_markdown:
$\sum r^{-k/2}=\sum \dfrac{1}{r^{k/2}}$ is a $p$-series with $p=\dfrac k2$. It converges if and only if $p>1$, that is $k>2$. It therefore diverges exactly when $p\le 1$:

$$\frac k2\le 1\iff k\le 2.$$

For $k\le 0$ the terms do not even tend to $0$, so the series still diverges, which is why the full set is $k\le2$ and not only $0<k\le2$ (option D is true but incomplete). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The image of the vector $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}$ under a mapping defined by the matrix $M$, where $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&2\\2&3&1\end{pmatrix}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The vector $\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-2\mathbf{k}$ has column form $(1,1,-2)^{T}$. Its image is

$$M\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot1+2\cdot1+3\cdot(-2)\\0\cdot1+1\cdot1+2\cdot(-2)\\2\cdot1+3\cdot1+1\cdot(-2)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-3\\3\end{pmatrix},$$

that is $-3\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The curve $C$ has parametric equations $x=a(t-\sin t)$, $y=a(1-\cos t)$, $a>0$, $0\le t\le 2\pi$. The area of the region bounded by the curve and the $x$-axis is $3\pi a^{2}$. The mean value of $y$ with respect to $x$ for $0\le t\le 2\pi$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The mean value of $y$ with respect to $x$ over an interval is $\dfrac{1}{x_2-x_1}\displaystyle\int y\,dx$, that is the area under the curve divided by the length of the $x$-interval.

When $t$ goes from $0$ to $2\pi$, $x$ goes from $0$ to $2\pi a$, so the interval has length $2\pi a$. With the given area $3\pi a^{2}$:

$$\bar y=\frac{3\pi a^{2}}{2\pi a}=\frac{3a}{2}.$$

(Check: $\int_0^{2\pi}a(1-\cos t)\cdot a(1-\cos t)\,dt=a^{2}\cdot 3\pi$.) Option A divides by $2\pi$ instead of by the length $2\pi a$ of the interval. **Answer: B.**
themes: mean and root mean square values

questions.enonce_markdown: A tangent at the pole to the polar curve $r=\sqrt2-2\cos\theta$ is $\theta=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The curve passes through the pole when $r=0$, and the tangent there is the line $\theta=\theta_0$ for a value $\theta_0$ with $r(\theta_0)=0$:

$$\sqrt2-2\cos\theta=0\iff\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\iff\theta=\pm\frac{\pi}{4}\ (\text{mod }2\pi).$$

Among the options only $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ appears (the other tangent at the pole is $\theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which one of the following conics is a parabola?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A conic is a parabola when exactly one variable is squared.

- A: $y=-x^{2}+4x-5=-(x-2)^{2}-1$, a parabola with vertex $(2,-1)$ opening downwards.
- B: $2(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}=6$, an ellipse.
- C: completing squares gives $4(x+4)^{2}-9(y+8)^{2}=36$, a hyperbola.
- D: $\dfrac{(x+2)^{2}}{36}-\dfrac{(y-1)^{2}}{25}=1$, a hyperbola.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the series $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{3}{r^{k+1}}$ converges, then
questions.corrige_markdown:
$\sum\dfrac{3}{r^{k+1}}=3\sum\dfrac{1}{r^{k+1}}$ is a constant multiple of a $p$-series with $p=k+1$. It converges if and only if $p>1$:

$$k+1>1\iff k>0.$$

Options C and D give sufficient conditions but not the exact condition, and option A would include $k=0$, where the series is the divergent harmonic series. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the group $(S=\{a,b,c,d\},\otimes)$

| $\otimes$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | $d$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $a$ | $d$ | $c$ | $b$ | $a$ |
| $b$ | $c$ | $d$ | $a$ | $b$ |
| $c$ | $b$ | $a$ | $d$ | $c$ |
| $d$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | $d$ |

The inverse of an element $x$, $x\in S$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The row of $d$ is $a,b,c,d$, so $d\otimes x=x=x\otimes d$ for every $x$: the identity element is $d$.

Reading the diagonal of the table: $a\otimes a=d$, $b\otimes b=d$, $c\otimes c=d$, $d\otimes d=d$. Every element composed with itself gives the identity, so every element is its own inverse:

$$x^{-1}=x\quad\text{for all }x\in S.$$

(This is the Klein four-group.) Option B would only be right for the identity $d$ itself, and options C and D would make the inverse depend on $x$, which the table contradicts. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f$, where
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k(1-x^{2}),&0\le x\le1\\0,&\text{elsewhere}\end{cases}$$
The cumulative probability function $F(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
$F(x)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt$. For $0<x\le1$:

$$F(x)=\int_0^{x}k(1-t^{2})\,dt=k\left(x-\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right).$$

For $x<0$ no probability has accumulated, so $F(x)=0$; for $x>1$ all of it has, so $F(x)=1$. (Normalisation gives $k\left(1-\tfrac13\right)=1$, so $k=\tfrac32$, consistent with $F(1)=1$.) Option A is the density, not the distribution function; options B and D drop the value $1$ for $x>1$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A particle of mass $m$ falls against a resistance of magnitude $kv$, where $v$ is the velocity and $k$ is a positive constant. The equation of motion is given by

*Options as printed:* A) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-mkv$   B) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv$   C) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=mg+kv$   D) $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=-mg-kv$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the downward direction as positive. The forces on the particle are its weight $mg$ downwards and the resistance $kv$ upwards, so Newton's second law gives

$$m\frac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{k}{m}v.$$

Options C and D have the wrong sign for the resistance (which opposes the motion), and option A has no weight term. Option B has the right structure but, as printed, the left-hand side lacks the factor $m$ ($\dfrac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv$ is not dimensionally consistent), so none of the printed options is exactly the equation of motion.

**Intended answer: $m\dfrac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv$ (the printed option B without its missing factor $m$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x$ is the displacement of a particle from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$, then which of the following represents oscillatory motion?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Solve each equation through its auxiliary equation.

- A: $m^{2}+4m+4=(m+2)^{2}=0$, so $x=(A+Bt)e^{-2t}$: critical damping, no oscillation.
- B: $m^{2}-4m-5=(m-5)(m+1)=0$, so $x=Ae^{5t}+Be^{-t}$: real exponentials.
- C: $m^{2}+4=0$, so $m=\pm2i$ and $x=A\cos2t+B\sin2t$: oscillation with period $\pi$ (simple harmonic motion).
- D: $m^{2}-4=0$, so $x=Ae^{2t}+Be^{-2t}$: real exponentials.

Oscillation requires complex roots, which only C has. **Answer: C.**
themes: simple harmonic motion of a particle

questions.enonce_markdown: If $f(x)=2+x^{2}-x^{3}$, then the equation $f(x)=0$ has a solution on the interval
questions.corrige_markdown:
$f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous, so the intermediate value theorem applies: a root lies in $[p,q]$ if $f(p)$ and $f(q)$ have opposite signs. Evaluate:

$$f(-2)=14,\quad f(-1)=4,\quad f(0)=2,\quad f(1)=2,\quad f(2)=2+4-8=-2.$$

Only on $[1,2]$ does the sign change ($f(1)=2>0$, $f(2)=-2<0$), so a root exists there (about $1.70$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{2\sin\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)}{x},&x\neq0\\ k,&x=0\end{cases}$ is a continuous function at $x=0$, the value of $k$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Continuity at $0$ requires $k=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}f(x)$. Using $\displaystyle\lim_{u\to0}\frac{\sin u}{u}=1$ with $u=\frac x2$:

$$\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2\sin\left(\frac x2\right)}{x}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin\left(\frac x2\right)}{\frac x2}=1.$$

So $k=1$. Option D is the trap of forgetting that $\sin(x/2)$ needs the argument $x/2$ in the denominator. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf{F}=(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})\,\mathrm{N}$ acts on a particle giving it a displacement of $(3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{k})\,\mathrm{m}$. The work done by $\mathbf{F}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Work done is the scalar product of force and displacement:

$$W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=(3)(3)+(-1)(0)+(2)(4)=9+0+8=17\ \mathrm J.$$

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The centre of symmetry of the curve $y=\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}-4}$, $x\neq\pm2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $f(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}-4}$. Its domain $\mathbb R\setminus\{\pm2\}$ is symmetric about $0$ and

$$f(-x)=\frac{-2x}{x^{2}-4}=-f(x),$$

so $f$ is an odd function. Its graph is therefore symmetric under a half-turn about the origin: the centre of symmetry is $(0,0)$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the truth table of a conjunction, then the values of $a$ and $b$ respectively are:

| $P$ | $Q$ | $P\wedge Q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | $a$ |
| F | T | F |
| F | F | $b$ |
questions.corrige_markdown: A conjunction $P\wedge Q$ is true only when both $P$ and $Q$ are true. In row 2, $Q$ is false, so $a=\mathrm F$. In row 4, both $P$ and $Q$ are false, so $b=\mathrm F$. Hence $(a,b)=(\mathrm F,\mathrm F)$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If two elastic spheres collide and the total mechanical energy remains constant, then the value of the coefficient of restitution $e$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: In a collision between two spheres, kinetic energy is lost unless the impact is perfectly elastic. The loss of kinetic energy is proportional to $(1-e^{2})$ (for direct impact it equals $\tfrac12\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}(1-e^{2})(u_1-u_2)^{2}$). If the total mechanical energy is conserved there is no loss, so $1-e^{2}=0$, that is $e=1$ (since $e\ge0$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4}[x]\,dx=$ , where $[x]$ is the greatest integer function of $x$
questions.corrige_markdown:
$[x]$ is constant on each interval $[n,n+1)$: it equals $0$ on $[0,1)$, $1$ on $[1,2)$, $2$ on $[2,3)$ and $3$ on $[3,4)$. Each interval has length $1$, so

$$\int_0^4[x]\,dx=0\cdot1+1\cdot1+2\cdot1+3\cdot1=6.$$

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of solution(s) of the equation $3\cosh(2x-1)=3$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Dividing by $3$: $\cosh(2x-1)=1$. The function $\cosh u$ has its minimum value $1$ at $u=0$ only, and $\cosh u>1$ for $u\neq0$. Hence

$$2x-1=0\iff x=\tfrac12,$$

and there is exactly one solution. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The coordinates of the point $P$ on the unit cube is

![fig-1](gce-al-further-maths-2020-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the figure the origin $O$ is the back lower left vertex; the $x$-axis points to the right, the $y$-axis upwards and the $z$-axis towards the viewer. The point $P$ is at the top of the back right edge: it is $1$ unit along $x$, $1$ unit up along $y$, and on the back face where $z=0$ (the front face is the one displaced towards $z$). Hence $P=(1,1,0)$.

The vertex $(1,1,1)$ would be the top front right corner, drawn lower and to the left of $P$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f(x)=\begin{cases}2\cosh x,&x<0\\ \sinh x,&x\ge0\end{cases}$ Then $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}f(x)$
questions.corrige_markdown:
A limit exists only if the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal.

$$\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to0^-}2\cosh x=2\cosh0=2,\qquad \lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=\lim_{x\to0^+}\sinh x=\sinh0=0.$$

Since $2\ne0$, the limit does not exist. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The depth of the cross-section of a river flowing at $2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ from riverbank to bank measures

| distance across, $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| depth, $y$ | $0.5$ | $1.2$ | $0.4$ |

A Simpson's rule approximation of the volume of water released each second is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The area of the cross-section (in $\mathrm{m^2}$) is $\int_0^2 y\,dx$. Simpson's rule with $2$ strips of width $h=1$:

$$A\approx\frac h3\big(y_0+4y_1+y_2\big)=\frac13\big(0.5+4(1.2)+0.4\big)=\frac{5.7}{3}=1.9\ \mathrm{m^{2}}.$$

The volume of water passing each second is the area times the speed of the river:

$$1.9\times2=3.8\ \mathrm{m^{3}/s}.$$

Option A ($7.6$) is what one gets by taking $h=2$ as the width of each strip, which doubles the area. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A parabola is the locus of a point equidistant from
questions.corrige_markdown: By definition, a parabola is the set of points $P$ whose distance from a fixed point (the focus) equals their distance from a fixed line (the directrix), that is, eccentricity $e=1$. Two fixed points give a straight line (perpendicular bisector), and two fixed lines give angle bisectors. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: a fixed point and a fixed line

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\cosh2x=\dfrac54$ then the positive value of $\sinh2x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $\cosh^{2}u-\sinh^{2}u=1$ with $u=2x$:

$$\sinh^{2}2x=\cosh^{2}2x-1=\frac{25}{16}-1=\frac{9}{16}\;\Rightarrow\;\sinh2x=\pm\frac34.$$

The positive value is $\dfrac34$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A medical treatment has a success rate of $90\%$. Two patients are administered the treatment independently. The probability that neither of them gets well is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Each patient fails to get well with probability $1-0.9=0.1$. By independence,

$$P(\text{neither gets well})=0.1\times0.1=0.01.$$

The value $0.81=0.9^{2}$ of option B is the probability that both get well. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The moment of inertia of a body of mass $3m$ about an axis is $9ma^{2}$. The radius of gyration of the body about the given axis is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The radius of gyration $k$ is defined by $I=Mk^{2}$, with $M=3m$ the mass of the body:

$$9ma^{2}=3m\,k^{2}\;\Rightarrow\;k^{2}=3a^{2}\;\Rightarrow\;k=a\sqrt3.$$

Option A comes from dividing by $m$ instead of $3m$ and then taking the root of $9a^2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The unit digit of the number $19^{2004}+11^{2004}-9^{2004}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The unit digit of a power depends only on the unit digit of the base, so work modulo $10$.

- $19\equiv9\pmod{10}$ and $9^{2}=81\equiv1$, so $9^{2004}=(9^{2})^{1002}\equiv1$. Hence $19^{2004}\equiv1$.
- $11\equiv1$, so $11^{2004}\equiv1$.
- $9^{2004}\equiv1$.

Therefore $19^{2004}+11^{2004}-9^{2004}\equiv1+1-1=1\pmod{10}$. The unit digit is $1$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The vertices $A,B,C$ of $\triangle ABC$ have position vectors $\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c$ respectively. The area of $\triangle ABC$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The area of a triangle is half the magnitude of the vector product of two of its sides. Take the sides $\overrightarrow{BA}=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=\mathbf b-\mathbf c$. Expanding option D:

$$(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)\times(\mathbf b-\mathbf c)=\mathbf a\times\mathbf b-\mathbf a\times\mathbf c-\mathbf b\times\mathbf b+\mathbf b\times\mathbf c=\mathbf a\times\mathbf b+\mathbf c\times\mathbf a+\mathbf b\times\mathbf c,$$

and this is exactly $(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c-\mathbf a)=\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$, whose magnitude is twice the area of the triangle. Option A gives the area of triangle $OAB$ only (with $O$ the origin), option B that of $OAC$, and option C is not meaningful ($\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\times\mathbf c$ is ambiguous). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is moving round the polar curve $r=1+\sin\theta$ with constant angular velocity $w$. The maximum speed of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
In polar coordinates the speed satisfies $v^{2}=\dot r^{2}+r^{2}\dot\theta^{2}$. Here $\dot\theta=w$ and $\dot r=\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\dot\theta=w\cos\theta$, so

$$v^{2}=w^{2}\big[\cos^{2}\theta+(1+\sin\theta)^{2}\big]=w^{2}\big[2+2\sin\theta\big].$$

This is greatest when $\sin\theta=1$ (that is $\theta=\tfrac\pi2$): $v^{2}_{\max}=4w^{2}$, so $v_{\max}=2w$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the function $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^{2}-1}{x+1},&x\neq-1\\ k,&x=-1\end{cases}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, then $k=$
questions.corrige_markdown: For $x\ne-1$, $\dfrac{x^{2}-1}{x+1}=\dfrac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x+1}=x-1$. Continuity at $x=-1$ requires $k=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-1}(x-1)=-2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $z=\big[i(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\big]^{n}$ then $\arg(z)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write $i=\cos\frac\pi2+i\sin\frac\pi2=e^{i\pi/2}$. Then

$$i(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=e^{i\pi/2}e^{i\theta}=e^{i\left(\theta+\frac\pi2\right)},$$

and by de Moivre's theorem

$$z=e^{in\left(\theta+\frac\pi2\right)}=\cos\!\left(n\theta+n\tfrac\pi2\right)+i\sin\!\left(n\theta+n\tfrac\pi2\right).$$

So $|z|=1$ and $\arg z=n\theta+n\dfrac\pi2$ (mod $2\pi$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The particular integral of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}-4\dfrac{dy}{dx}+4y=e^{2x}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The auxiliary equation is $m^{2}-4m+4=(m-2)^{2}=0$: a repeated root $m=2$, so the complementary function is $(A+Bx)e^{2x}$. The right-hand side $e^{2x}$ already contains $e^{2x}$ and $xe^{2x}$, so the trial particular integral must be multiplied by $x^{2}$:

$$y_p=\lambda x^{2}e^{2x}.$$

(Check: $y_p''-4y_p'+4y_p=2\lambda e^{2x}$, so $\lambda=\tfrac12$.) Options A and B are solutions of the homogeneous equation and would give $0$ on the left-hand side. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $f(x)$ is a continuous even function, then $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Split the integral at $0$: $\int_{-a}^{a}f=\int_{-a}^{0}f+\int_{0}^{a}f$. In the first integral substitute $u=-x$; since $f(-u)=f(u)$ for an even function,

$$\int_{-a}^{0}f(x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(-u)\,du=\int_{0}^{a}f(u)\,du.$$

Hence $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^af(x)\,dx$. (Option A holds for an odd function.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y=0$ and $y=1$ when $x=0$. A quadratic approximation for $y$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the Maclaurin expansion $y\approx y(0)+xy'(0)+\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}y''(0)$.

From the equation, $y'=-2y$, so $y'(0)=-2$. Differentiating, $y''=-2y'=4y$, so $y''(0)=4$. Hence

$$y\approx1-2x+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\cdot4=1-2x+2x^{2}.$$

(This agrees with the exact solution $y=e^{-2x}=1-2x+2x^{2}-\cdots$.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The function $f$ has a removable discontinuity at $x_0$. Therefore
questions.corrige_markdown:
A discontinuity is removable when $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to x_0}f(x)$ exists (and is finite) but $f$ is not continuous there, either because $f(x_0)$ is undefined or because $f(x_0)$ differs from the limit. We can then redefine $f(x_0)$ as the limit to remove the discontinuity.

- A is not necessary: $f(x_0)$ may be undefined.
- C would mean $f$ is continuous at $x_0$.
- D describes a jump or infinite discontinuity.

Only B is always true. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $x>0$, then $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\ln\sinh2x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
By the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=\sinh2x$ and $u'=2\cosh2x$:

$$\frac{d}{dx}\ln\sinh2x=\frac{2\cosh2x}{\sinh2x}=2\coth2x.$$

Option A forgets the factor $2$ from the inner derivative. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{x^{2}}{x^{2}-1}$ expressed in partial fractions, where $P,Q$, and $R$, are real constants, with $x\neq\pm1$, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The numerator and the denominator have the same degree ($2$), so the fraction is improper: divide first.

$$\frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}-1}=1+\frac{1}{x^{2}-1}=1+\frac{1}{(x-1)(x+1)}=1+\frac{1/2}{x-1}-\frac{1/2}{x+1}.$$

So the form is $P+\dfrac{Q}{x+1}+\dfrac{R}{x-1}$ with $P=1$, $Q=-\tfrac12$, $R=\tfrac12$. The factors $x-1$ and $x+1$ are distinct, so no squared denominator appears. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is executing simple harmonic motion with amplitude $2$ metres and period $12$ seconds. What is the maximum speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$ of the particle?
questions.corrige_markdown:
For simple harmonic motion $x=a\sin(\omega t+\varepsilon)$ with period $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$ and amplitude $a$, the maximum speed is $a\omega$.

$$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{12}=\frac{\pi}{6},\qquad v_{\max}=a\omega=2\cdot\frac\pi6=\frac\pi3\ \mathrm{m/s}.$$

Option A forgets the factor $a=2$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which one of the following linear Diophantine equations has positive solutions?
questions.corrige_markdown: Look for solutions in positive integers $x,y\ge1$. Then $x+5y\ge1+5=6$, so the right-hand side must be at least $6$. Only $x+5y=7$ qualifies, with $y=1$, $x=2$ (check: $2+5=7$). For $3$, $2$ and $1$ the smallest possible value $6$ is already too large, so there is no positive solution. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf F=(2\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-\mathbf k)\,\mathrm N$ displaces a particle through $(12\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)\,\mathrm m$. The work done by the force is
questions.corrige_markdown:
$$W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=(2)(12)+(4)(4)+(-1)(2)=24+16-2=38\ \mathrm J.$$

Option D, $|\mathbf F||\mathbf d|=\sqrt{21}\sqrt{164}\approx58.7$, would be the work if the force were parallel to the displacement, which it is not. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $|x|>2$, then $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}-4}}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the standard result $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}}=\cosh^{-1}\!\left(\frac xa\right)+k$ (for $x>a$), with $a=2$:

$$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}-4}}=\cosh^{-1}\!\left(\frac x2\right)+k.$$

Check by differentiating: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cosh^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac x2\right)=\dfrac{1/2}{\sqrt{x^{2}/4-1}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}-4}}$. The inverse sine in B belongs to $\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{4-x^{2}}}$, and the inverse hyperbolic tangent in D to $\int\dfrac{dx}{4-x^{2}}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The furthest point from the pole to the polar curve $r=2+\sqrt2\sin\theta$ occurs when $\theta=$
questions.corrige_markdown: The distance from the pole is $|r|=2+\sqrt2\sin\theta$, which is positive for all $\theta$ because $2>\sqrt2$. It is greatest when $\sin\theta=1$, that is $\theta=\dfrac\pi2$, where $r=2+\sqrt2\approx3.41$. At $\theta=-\dfrac\pi2$ it is smallest ($2-\sqrt2$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A point $P$ traces the curve $r=a\theta$, $O$ the pole, such that $OP$ moves with constant angular velocity $w$. The radial component of acceleration when $P$ is at the point $(r,\theta)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
In polar coordinates the radial component of acceleration is $\ddot r-r\dot\theta^{2}$. Here $\dot\theta=w$ is constant, so $\ddot\theta=0$, and

$$\dot r=a\dot\theta=aw,\qquad\ddot r=a\ddot\theta=0.$$

Hence the radial component is $0-rw^{2}=-rw^{2}$. (The transverse component is $r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta=2aw^{2}$, which is the value in option D.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $f(x)=2x+|x-2|-|x|$ and $0\le x<2$, then $f(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $0\le x<2$ we have $x-2<0$, so $|x-2|=2-x$, and $x\ge0$, so $|x|=x$. Therefore

$$f(x)=2x+(2-x)-x=2.$$

So $f$ is constant on this interval. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The component of the force $(3\mathbf i-\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)\,\mathrm N$ in the direction of the vector $(-4\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The component of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf d$ is $\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf d}=\dfrac{\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|}$. Here

$$\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=(3)(0)+(-1)(-4)+(2)(3)=10,\qquad|\mathbf d|=\sqrt{16+9}=5,$$

so the component is $\dfrac{10}{5}=2$. Option A forgets to divide by $|\mathbf d|$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The area of a square, $A(t)$, is increasing at a rate equal to its perimeter. $A(t)$ satisfies the differential equation $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let the side of the square be $s$. Then $A=s^{2}$, so $s=\sqrt A$, and the perimeter is $4s=4\sqrt A$. The area increases at a rate equal to the perimeter, so

$$\frac{dA}{dt}=4\sqrt A.$$

The minus sign in option C would mean a decreasing area. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that the moment of inertia of a rod of mass $m$ and length $2l$ about an axis through its centre perpendicular to the rod is $I$, then the moment of inertia about a perpendicular axis on the rod distant $x$ from the centre is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The perpendicular axis through a point of the rod at distance $x$ from the centre is parallel to the axis through the centre of mass. By the parallel axes theorem, $I_{\text{new}}=I_G+mx^{2}$, where $I_G=I$ is the moment of inertia about the parallel axis through the centre of mass:

$$I_{\text{new}}=I+mx^{2}.$$

(With $I=\tfrac13ml^{2}$ for this rod this is $\tfrac13ml^{2}+mx^{2}$; option A subtracts instead of adding, and option D wrongly divides $I$ by $3$.) **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: How many proper subgroups are there in a cyclic group of order $12$?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A cyclic group of order $12$ has exactly one subgroup for each divisor of $12$, namely of orders $1,2,3,4,6,12$. Excluding the whole group (order $12$) and the trivial subgroup $\{e\}$ (order $1$), the proper (non-trivial) subgroups have orders $2,3,4,6$: there are $4$ of them.

With the convention that only the group itself is excluded one would count $5$ (including $\{e\}$), a value that is not offered, so the convention used here is that proper means different from both $\{e\}$ and $G$. **Answer: A.**
